title: England 26-26 Canada: Red Roses' 39-game winning run ends with thrilling draw
description: WXV Global SeriesEngland (19) 26Tries: Moloney-MacDonald 2, Botterman, Field Cons: Harrison 3Canada (19) 26Tries: Gibson, Menin 2 Cons: De Goede 3Engl
body: WXV Global SeriesEngland (19) 26Tries: Moloney-MacDonald 2, Botterman, Field Cons: Harrison 3Canada (19) 26Tries: Gibson, Menin 2 Cons: De Goede 3England's remarkable 39-match winning run came to an end as they were held to a nail-biting 26-26 draw by Canada at Sandy Park.The Red Roses were unable to escape the clutches of a relentless Canada, who they beat in last year's World Cup final, with the two sides sharing four tries apiece in front of a raucous 14,573 crowd in Exeter.Canada are the first team to avoid defeat against England since New Zealand beat them in the 2022 World Cup final, but John Mitchell's side are now unbeaten in 40 Tests.The draw also ended England's 100% home record against Canada, having won each of their previous 13 home meetings.In a pulsating opening 25 minutes, England were twice required to come from behind, with tries from Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and Hannah Botterman cancelling out scores by Lizzie Gibson and DaLeaka Menin for Canada.Exeter winger Moloney-MacDonald had a try disallowed before giving England the lead for the first time in the 32nd minute, getting on the end of a surging run from Sadia Kabeya for her second of the match.However, Canada - who had earlier had a brilliant solo effort from Asia Hogan-Rochester chalked off for a forward pass - hit back on the stroke of half-time when Menin crashed over from close range.England weathered 10 minutes of sustained pressure at the beginning of the second half before the two sides exchanged tries again, prop Bryony Field restoring the lead for the hosts before Canada scrum-half Olivia Apps scored under the posts after a dancing run from Sophie de Goede down the left wing.England looked the most likely to win in a chaotic final 10 minutes, including being held up over the line, but were left to a rue a turnover in front of the posts and a loose carry as Canada battled through for the draw.The two sides will resume their rivalry with two Tests in Canada in October.Before then, England face New Zealand at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham on Saturday, 26 September.England's run of 39 consecutive wins, which started in March 2023, encompassed four successive Women's Six Nations crowns, two WXV1 successes and a home World Cup triumph in 2025.But all things must come to an end.It is not that England have not been tested in that time. A week earlier, Australia led 10-5 at half-time, marking the first time the Red Roses had trailed at the interval since 2020.France have often been a thorn in their side in Six Nations deciders too, while Canada ran them close in a WXV meeting in 2024.The challenge for opponents has been sustaining that pressure for a full 80-minute performance, and Canada did not let up at Sandy Park.Twice they led, twice they were pegged back. There was an ominous feeling when Moloney-MacDonald put the hosts in front, but Canada seized their opportunity, capitalising on back-to-back penalties in England's 22 to level.On the back foot as England - energised by their replacements - pressed for the win, they responded twice more, first cancelling out Field's try and then doggedly defending in their own half for much of the final 20 minutes.As impressive as Canada were in defence, England were also left to rue the lack of a clinical touch in Canada's 22 and opted against kicking for three points when awarded a penalty in the closing stages.But rather than be disappointed, head coach Mitchell hailed the opportunity that the result presents."Canada were good and we were also good," he said. "At times it was a real arm wrestle."We are really in a Test series, which is great for us. Canada need to be congratulated on their performance."For us, it's about getting better and there is a greater purpose than just one Test match. This is ideal for us and allows us to stay focused on what's necessary to get a better performance."Speaking before the match, Canada captain De Goede said recollections of last year's World Cup final defeat has kept her awake "four to five nights a week".Even after snapping the world champions' record unbeaten run, De Goede contemplated what might have been."There's definitely some frustration that we didn't get the win in the end, but also we're moving in the right direction from the last time we played them," said the second row forward."We need to be critical of ourselves after the game because I do think we could have got the win."We know we can get it across the line and that's where the disappointment comes from. There's a lot of pride in our defensive stance in the last 20 minutes, but we really struggled to exit, so we'll have to watch back what we were doing on the attacking side of the ball."With the clock in the red, Canada had a scrum near to their own 22 and De Goede said the players on the field were keen to keep the game alive, but afterwards the skipper reluctantly conceded that coach Kevin Rouet made the right call by instructing them to kick to touch and end the match."The plan on the field - we were like 'let's go for the win'," said De Goede. "Then the message came on from the sideline to kick it out."I do trust Kevin, he has the cooler head in that moment. If we gave away a penalty off the next breakdown, we'd be sitting here going 'why didn't you kick it out?'"England: Kildunne; Breach, Jones (capt), Rowland, Moloney-MacDonald; Harrison, L Packer; Botterman, Field, Muir, Talling, Ives Campion, Burton, Kabeya, Matthews.Replacements: Campbell, Carson, Bern, Burns, Feaunati, M Packer, Robinson, Aitchison. Canada: Gallagher; Hogan-Rochester, Symonds, Tessier, Williams; Perry, Apps; Nelson, Idowu, Menin, De Goede (capt), Royer, Smith, Omokhuale, Gibson. Replacements: Boag, McDonald, Rempel, Forteza, Buisa, Senft, Pelletier, Bauder.

schema.headline: England 26-26 Canada: Red Roses' 39-game winning run ends with thrilling draw

title: Tottenham 2-3 Aston Villa: No sign of recovery from struggling Spurs
description: Tottenham have failed to win any of their last 36 Premier League matches when conceding first so the writing was on the wall at half-time.They dominat
body: Tottenham have failed to win any of their last 36 Premier League matches when conceding first so the writing was on the wall at half-time.They dominated the opening 20 minutes and Villa keeper Zion Suzuki denied Savio and Archie Gray but, without a goal, they were always going to be vulnerable at the other end.And so, in first-half injury time, a Villa goal was almost inevitable. Andy Robertson tried to stop a corner but only gifted the ball to John McGinn and, after Boubacar Kamara's effort, Manzambi prodded in from close range. It added the insult to Van de Ven's injury, a blow to the face that kept him off the pitch.Some Tottenham fans missed the goal as they headed for their half-time refreshments but several thousand did not bother to stay until the end.They streamed out of the stands after Buendia's brilliant 25-yard bullet found the top corner in the 79th minute, missing Gallagher and Van Hecke's late efforts.De Zerbi said: "My focus is why we concede the first goal with 10 players, we can stay stronger, communicate more and more, defend in a compact way."I put [Rodrigo] Bentancur as a centre-back in that minute and Mateus Fernandes as a midfielder. If we have a red card we can play 70 minutes with 10 players."In the second half we scored the goal with [Mohammed] Kudus, offside, I don't know if some players lost energy but we conceded an unacceptable goal. We knew this season Aston Villa are playing 86% more long balls than last season."We had many meetings [about it] and we have to explain another game like Newcastle where we played the first half well and then we lose. It's my responsibility. "I take my responsibility but in that moment of the game we have to defend, we have to defend compact, the leaders have to be leaders."I am very sad and frustrated with the performance. We cannot lose this game in this way. The second goal we conceded was incredible.""Sacked in the morning" chanted the Villa fans to De Zerbi who, at times, looked out of ideas once his side fell 2-0 behind. It was Tottenham's worst start to a top-flight season since 2008-09, when they also had two points after five games. Juande Ramos was dismissed as manager after three more defeats before Harry Redknapp lifted them up to eighth. Spurs have also now gone five league games without a win at the start of a season for the first time since 1986.Former Brighton striker Glenn Murray, however, says De Zerbi needs time."He is trying to build something, it will take time," he told BBC's Final Score. "Taking the emotion out of it, looking at the stats, they have had more shots in three of the past four games, more possession and more touches in the opposition box."They are positives, be patient, the metrics are there to say he will turn it around. They need to be patient with Roberto De Zerbi, with all the signings, it takes time to gel and get to know each other."A decisive moment came when Kudus thought he had levelled on the hour, but Robertson was ruled just offside having delivered the cross. Seven minutes later Jackson scored from Suzuki's long launch downfield and it was game over.Villa's rebuild, the club committing to spending more than £250m was out of necessity because of their own high-profile exits. There was an expectation change was forthcoming and the Europa League winners were always going to go through a period of transition.But a first league victory was vital for them too after three defeats in their opening four games. While Villa look in better shape as new players settle, Spurs have thrown money at their problems after two relegation battles, but are no closer to solving them. Sandro Tonali, the £100m midfielder from Newcastle, was overshadowed by Villa's tenacious skipper McGinn - a £2.75m buy from Hibs eight years ago.Brazil winger Savio was denied three times by the impressive Suzuki but faded, while Omar Marmoush was signed to bring goals, but provided nothing. De Zerbi added: "I didn't speak with the players [afterwards], I didn't want to say anything. The players who go to the national team, they have to play and work. "The others, [James] Maddison, Gallagher, [Dominic] Solanke, Tosin [Adarabioyo, [Marcos] Senesi, Savio have to work more because their physical condition, I didn't like in this game."Former Chelsea and England midfielder Joe Cole questioned Tottenham's transfer business after their spend of around £302m.After Tonali, £85m went on bringing in Mateus Fernandes from West Ham. The Portuguese midfielder was subbed at half-time and De Zerbi said he "didn't like" Fernandes' performance, while £75m was spent on Savio from Manchester City. Marmoush will cost £60m once his loan becomes permanent but Spurs need their big-money buys to prove their worth and perform sooner rather than later."Spurs are dominant, chances, and you felt the tension growing - all of a sudden Spurs were just wanting to get to half-time. Once you defend with anxiety, things happen," Cole told TNT. "When these things go against you, they go against you, Van de Ven going off was a factor, they didn't deal with it well, when you are anxious you make rash decisions. "Villa defended well but didn't deserve to go in a goal up, and then this place deflated."They are not picking up points, a club flirting with relegation two years in a row, I feel they have overpaid for every player they bought this summer - you can't rule them out from being in and around the relegation battle."De Zerbi, though, defended their summer window despite their current malaise."I am happy with the squad but the market was long, the situation changed many times," he said."There was also financial fair play and we have to respect that. We didn't sell the players we thought there was a possibility to sell. "The club and the coach, we are not sleeping, we know the characteristics of the players. If we didn't make any different decisions it was because we couldn't."

title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico say reporters denied White House access after Trump banned some media outlets
description: "The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled," MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said. "I asked why I was not able to get in
body: "The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled," MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said. "I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him."Gardner added that while her and her colleague's badges were disabled, an MS NOW producer was still able to scan her badge to get in, though she was not given an explanation as to why the producer's badge still worked.CNN reporter Betsy Klein said a Secret Service agent told her her badge had been deactivated.Later on Saturday morning, Politico said its reporter Cheyenne Haslett was denied entry and Secret Service revoked her pass. All three outlets have spoken out against the decision, accusing Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press.An MS NOW spokesperson said in a statement that the White House "belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars".MS NOW said it "intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy".Politico Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger said in an internal email, shared in the outlet's Playbook newsletter, that the company stands by its reporters and will "vigorously defend" their First Amendment rights. And CNN said, "We have a right under the US Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right."In his announcement, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting from the three outlets that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years".Trump added that there "may be others to join them", but has not given a directive banning additional news outlets. When later asked by a reporter what he meant by others to come, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news."Several groups dedicated to the freedom of the press have called out Trump's White House ban as illegal and unconstitutional.A major group that provides legal services to the media - the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press - said it expected Trump's ban to be struck down quickly by the courts because it was "flatly unconstitutional"."The First Amendment is clear that once the White House invites in some journalists, it can't ban others because it doesn't like their reporting," said Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, which provides legal services to the media.It's the latest in a series of moves by the administration to target media outlets Trump says are critical of him, including legal action against US and international outlets like The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and the BBC.Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multimillion dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.Additional reporting from Bernd Debusmann Jr and Max Matza.

schema.headline: CNN, MS NOW and Politico say reporters denied White House access after Trump banned some media outlets

title: Perth shark attack: Rare kill order issued as victim identified as Greg O'Neill
description: A rare catch-and-kill order has been issued for a great white shark off the coast of Western Australia after 63-year-old swimmer Greg O'Neill was kill
body: A rare catch-and-kill order has been issued for a great white shark off the coast of Western Australia after 63-year-old swimmer Greg O'Neill was killed at a popular beach on Friday. His body has still not been found.Authorities have said that beaches along the state's coast, including in the capital Perth, will remain closed until at least Sunday as the search for the shark continues.It is the second shark attack in Western Australia (WA) this week, and the third fatal attack in the state this year.The incident, at Sorrento Beach in Perth's north, has reignited debate about how to keep beachgoers safe in Australia.In a statement, Greg O'Neill's family said they were "deeply shocked and devastated by the terrible tragedy.""Greg loved the ocean and was known as a passionate swimmer, sports lover, dedicated worker and an all-round generous, witty guy."On Saturday, his family visited the scene, where locals have been laying flowers.Witness Jacqui Rapaic told the ABC that two men were swimming, but only one made it back to shore, and that she could see "a pool of blood" in the water.Another witness told WAtoday that she saw the man being "mauled" as the shark "tossed him around like a fish". Members of the public reported seeing a 2.5m-long (8ft 2in) shark at around the same time.Joondalup authorities, where Sorrento is located, said all beaches were closed "as a precautionary measure" and would remain so until at least midday on Sunday.Pictures on Saturday showed the coastline being patrolled by a police boat and helicopter.Catch-and-kill orders are rare and controversial in Australia, where great white sharks are a protected species.WA Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis said that she took the "extraordinary step" of issuing the order after the shark was spotted by water police on Saturday morning, and "positively identified as the shark involved in the incident".The minister said she authorised fisheries officers to "destroy the shark" if it could be captured because of the "exceptional circumstances" of the attack and the "hazard posed by the shark".It is believed to be the first time in 10 years that such an order had been issued in WA, Jarvis added, emphasising that the order was not a widespread cull as the state has seen in the past.The minister also said that the use of drones and tagging would be increased to help protect beachgoers.Catching and killing sharks has a long and controversial history in Western Australia - there were months of huge protests in 2014 when the state government authorised a cull after a spate of attacks.The incident in Sorrento is the second in WA this week - on Monday a 56-year-old man was bitten while surfing off the coast of Geraldton, 430km (270 miles) north of Perth. He survived but lost part of his leg, another surfer who rescued him told the ABC.There have been five fatal shark attacks in Australia this year. A 12-year-old boy died after he was bitten in Sydney Harbour in January, and three divers were fatally mauled in separate incidents between May and June - two in Western Australia and the third in Queensland.

schema.headline: Perth shark attack: Rare kill order issued as victim identified as Greg O'Neill

title: September reset: Why now is the time to start a new routine and how to stick to it
description: For Cami, a content creator and podcast host from Northampton, September spells the end of summer spontaneity and a time to restore order."If you've b
body: For Cami, a content creator and podcast host from Northampton, September spells the end of summer spontaneity and a time to restore order."If you've been away for the summer you've probably not had a massive routine," she says. "And if you're a parent, then you've got kids at home and it's just a bit more chaotic," she says.September feels like "back to school...getting back into your own rhythm", she adds.It is the perfect time to "get everything sorted", she says "So when you get to January you're not trying to do everything at once.For Bas Verplanken, professor emeritus of social psychology at the University of Bath, September is a chance to "reorient yourself".He says his research suggests people who experienced a big change such as moving house "were more responsive to an intervention aimed at promoting sustainable behaviours" than comparable people who had not moved house."It's really an exciting way of looking at disruption," he told Chris and Xand van Tulleken on their What's Up Docs? podcast.If your daily commute or school run works for you then relax back into them."But if there are alternative ways of doing things, explore it, this is the time to do it, and to make those changes," says Verplanken.Cami says planning is key - something she does on a Sunday morning. "I go, okay, these are my meals for the week. These are my workouts for the week. Even plan your outfits for the work day if you really want to because it saves you time," she says.Then she takes steps to "limit the choices" she has to stray from her routine."I will meal prep three days worth of overnight oats. Naturally, I'm going to grab those in the morning because they are made and ready. I've removed the friction of grabbing a quick meal or not having any breakfast."Verplanken agrees the secret to making new habits that last is setting yourself up so that your new behaviours are the easiest option for reaching your goal.He advises designing a routine where your habits can become "effortless"."They are specific plans of where, when, and what you will do," he says."Let's say, losing weight, you can think when I go to the supermarket, I'm going to look specifically each time [at] the fat and sugar content [of food]. It's a very specific plan."This means making the right choices when are facing the food shelf happen automatically "because you have already planned the situation in which you have to act".If this is done frequently, Verplanken says it becomes "extremely effective" to turn these habits into your routine.

schema.headline: September reset: Why now is the time to start a new routine and how to stick to it

title: Houthis claim attack on Riyadh after fire near airport
description: Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen say they carried out drone and missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh and energy sites on the country's Red
body: Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen say they carried out drone and missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh and energy sites on the country's Red Sea coast.  A column of black smoke was seen rising from what appeared to be fuel tanks near the Saudi capital's international airport on Saturday, hours after air raid alerts were issued.It was the first time residents had been given an alert and urged to stay indoors since a recent escalation in the conflict with the Houthis.There has been no official comment from Saudi authorities.In a statement posted online, Houthi military spokesman Yahya al-Sarea said a "large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones" had been used to attack "sensitive sites" in Riyadh and Aramco state oil and gas company facilities in Yanbu on the coast.  He added that the attacks were "in response to the Saudi enemy's criminal attempts" to target the Yemeni capital Sanaa.Earlier, Sarea had accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out 300 strikes across Yemen during the past week.The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.They have attacked targets inside Saudi Arabia on several occasions in recent months, and said this week that they were responsible for downing a Saudi fighter jet over Yemen.According to an unconfirmed report from AFP news agency, quoting military sources on both sides of Yemen's civil war, fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces claimed 48 lives on Saturday.The Houthis said 31 of their fighters had been killed while government sources said their side had lost 17 soldiers, according to the news agency.      On Friday, the International Organization for Migration, a UN body, reported that the number of people displaced as a result of recent fighting had passed 104,796, external.A number of apparent explosions were heard in Riyadh and major problems were reported at King Khalid International Airport earlier on Saturday, with the tracking website FlightRadar24 reporting delays and cancellations., externalAn AFP journalist reported that firefighters could be seen trying to extinguish the flames of a burnt-out fuel tank belonging to Aramco.The Saudi Civil Defence had sent out phone alerts overnight warning of potential danger in Riyadh and other regions, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning.Residents told AFP on condition of anonymity that they had heard what sounded like a round of explosions echoing through the city after the alerts."I heard the alarm, then my windows shook," said a resident of northern Riyadh, 27. "It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this."The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island, a gateway to a key shipping route used by the Gulf state to export to Asia and Europe.The group said the naval blockade was in retaliation for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled north-western Yemen.Saudi vessels have relied on that stretch of the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.      On Friday, investment banking giant JP Morgan said it was struggling to predict how oil prices would be impacted by the war, telling investors in a rare note that "we simply don't know how to model the endgame".

schema.headline: Houthis claim attack on Riyadh after fire near airport

title: US and Denmark reach deal over Greenland's security after Trump threats
description: The US and Denmark have announced a deal on Greenland's security, resolving a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Donald Trump's threats to seize
body: The US and Denmark have announced a deal on Greenland's security, resolving a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Donald Trump's threats to seize it by force.Nato said the deal would help stabilise the region, as Trump said Denmark would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in the semi-autonomous Danish territory.The leaders of Denmark and Greenland welcomed the deal to "strengthen security", which they said was expected to be signed next week, but did not outline its contents.The deal comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic location for defence purposes and its mineral wealth.No text of the agreement has been released. Trump said the deal came with "no cost to the United States" and would grant it the ability "to do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland", in a post on Truth Social.He said it included a rule that no US adversary could maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval".A Nato spokesperson said the military alliance welcomed the deal, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region".Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week.The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted.Nielsen said it was "gratifying that we are about to enter into an agreement that ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western alliance"."The agreement recognises Greenland's interests and our place in international co-operation. It is for the benefit of us all," he said.Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China. His repeated demands to take Greenland earlier this year prompted an outcry from Greenlanders, Danes and other Nato members.There is hope the crisis has now been brought to an end, with some Danish media interpreting the agreement as a quiet but significant triumph for the country's diplomacy."Don't tell Trump that it's the Kingdom of Denmark that has won," read one headline in the newspaper Berlingske on Saturday."Trump didn't get Greenland, but he was allowed to take a victory lap on social media," wrote a US correspondent for Politiken. Territorial integrity was a red line for Denmark and Greenland, and the US president has made no mention of any territory changing hands.It is not yet clear what concessions or sweeteners, if any, have been agreed - and in Greenland, some are still nervous."[It's] news we have all been hoping for," MP Naaja Nathanielsen wrote on social media. But she added: "It is absolutely crucial that any agreement preserves our right to self-determination."Former Greenlandic politician Aaja Chemnitz said she looked forward to the deal being finalised, but "until then, I'm sceptical". "I don't have much confidence in Trump," she said.The text of the agreement has not been published. The BBC has contacted the Danish Embassy in the US and the White House.However, an unnamed US State Department official outlined the deal without providing specifics.Among the agreed provisions is one stating the deal would not expire even if Greenland became an independent country in the future.The official added that under the deal, the US has unilateral power to build additional military structures with no approval needed from Greenland or Denmark. It includes "permanent access, basing and overflights rights," the official said.It also bans non-Nato countries from building bases in Greenland, and "bans adversaries from making investments in Greenland that could threaten the United States".The official added that under the current status quo, adversaries have been allowed to invest in Greenland's "sensitive sectors without investment screening".The official specifically referenced Russia and China, saying it blocks them from deploying troops or making investments in "sensitive sectors".

schema.headline: US and Denmark reach deal over Greenland's security after Trump threats

title: Trump ramps up feud with press after week of setbacks
description: The president's frustration at the media, however, came after a week of setbacks in which major institutions handed him a series of losses across his
body: The president's frustration at the media, however, came after a week of setbacks in which major institutions handed him a series of losses across his agenda.First, the Supreme Court blocked his plan to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the midterms. This prompted Trump to lash out at the court's justices including those he had appointed. "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," he said.The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, then raised interest rates after Trump had spent months arguing they should be cut. This was followed by a judge ordering his administration to give 30 days' notice before making any changes to the Kennedy Center arts venue in Washington DC after the president warned it could be "ripped down".These headlines, combined with approval ratings that recently sunk to record lows for his second term, suggest Trump is facing challenging political headwinds.His latest attack on the press, however, raises clear legal questions. The First Amendment to the US Constitution forbids Congress from "abridging" the freedom of the press. It is language that courts have long interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.All three targeted news outlets have promised to file lawsuits challenging Trump's decision.Although the breadth of this move is unprecedented, it is far from the first time the Trump administration has attempted to limit or deny access to the White House to members of mainstream media outlets.In his first term, the administration revoked CNN correspondent Jim Acosta's press credentials, setting off a legal battle that was ultimately resolved in the journalist's favour. It also temporarily suspended the pass of a reporter who had a heated argument with White House adviser Sebastian Gorka – a move that also was subsequently blocked by the courts.Last year, the White House banned reporters for the Associated Press from participating in the president's press pool - which allows media outlets access to smaller in-town and travelling presidential appearances - because the newswire service would not follow Trump's move to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.That dispute also led to a protracted - and yet to be fully resolved - legal battle, prompting the White House to change press pool rules to drop the guaranteed spot for all wire services.The White House bans, however, represent a dramatic escalation. The restrictions include access to the entirety of the White House grounds, not just the press pool. And they target entire news organisations, not just a single disfavoured correspondent.While Trump has been clear about the motives behind his decision, he has shed little light on why he has acted now. He has regularly criticised his press coverage since he first entered national politics more than a decade ago, but he said on Friday there was no specific incident that prompted his announcement.At the moment, however, the president is embattled. Even beyond the week of clear setbacks, he is in the midst of an unpopular and difficult-to-resolve war of choice in Iran, which has led to a surge in energy and other consumer prices, deflating his standing with the American public.Polls also suggest his party faces an uphill battle to retain control of the House of Representatives and perhaps the Senate in November's crucial midterm congressional elections.His attempts to improve the public's mood by touting his accomplishments in campaign events and at his Republican Party's convention earlier this month in Texas have, at least so far, proven ineffective.There may be more behind the Trump's decision to lash out at the media this weekend. But it could also simply be an indication of presidential frustration in the face of events and circumstances, some of his own making, that are turning against him.

schema.headline: Trump ramps up feud with press after week of setbacks

title: England vs Sri Lanka: Harry Brook and Jos Buttler lead hosts to top of rankings
description: Third T20 international, Old TraffordSri Lanka 124 all out (18.5 overs): Nissanka 36 (24), K Mendis 35 (28); Baker 2-17, Archer 2-23, Jacks 2-31Englan
body: Third T20 international, Old TraffordSri Lanka 124 all out (18.5 overs): Nissanka 36 (24), K Mendis 35 (28); Baker 2-17, Archer 2-23, Jacks 2-31England 126-2 (9.4 overs): Buttler 62* (32), Brook 33 (21)England won by eight wickets, won series 3-0ScorecardEngland steamrollered Sri Lanka in the third T20 to complete a 3-0 series clean sweep and return to number one in the world rankings.Watched by new Test coach Stephen Fleming, England once again outclassed the tourists to conclude a one-sided series played on the fringe of autumn.England's pace bowlers were outstanding in dismissing Sri Lanka for a paltry 124, then the home side chased the target in 9.4 overs.Jamie Overton conceded only 15 runs in his four overs, including taking a wicket. Sonny Baker's improvement continued with 2-17 and Jofra Archer recovered from an expensive start to return 2-23.England's fielding was sharp, best demonstrated by Liam Dawson's direct hit to run out Eshan Malinga.The target was never likely to pose a challenge to an England batting line-up that remains powerful despite Phil Salt and Jacob Bethell being absent injured.Though opener Aneurin Donald was out for 13, Jos Buttler and Harry Brook strolled the pursuit with a second-wicket stand of 85.Brook was run out for 33, leaving Buttler to wrap it up with a six that left him unbeaten on 61.The victory by eight wickets was concluded with 62 balls to spare - the most for England in a home T20 international.The success was England's 23rd win in 26 completed T20s since Brook took charge in the summer of 2024. They have reclaimed their number one ranking from India.The pity for this group is a rare lengthy wait until the next global T20 tournament. The next men's T20 World Cup is not until 2028, the same year T20 cricket makes its debut in the Olympics.England are instead building towards a 50-over World Cup in southern Africa in the autumn of 2027. Three one-day internationals against the Sri Lankans begin in Durham on Tuesday.A feature of England's success in this format has been captain Brook's heavy use of spin bowling. On this occasion the spinners took a backseat – Adil Rashid and Dawson sent down only four overs between them.Instead, it was the seamers to the fore, even without the variations of Sam Curran, another England player absent injured.Baker endured difficult debuts in all three international formats, yet in this series has started to show his potential.After Archer's first over went for 15, Baker had Lahiru Udara sky to wicketkeeper Buttler. He later returned to wrap up the innings, taking the final wicket when Dilshan Madushanka skied to Brook.Archer was a spectator for some time after his initial struggle. When he returned, he got the dangerous Kamindu Mendis to pull to deep mid-wicket for 35. Archer's second wicket was curious – Wanindu Hasaranga out hit-wicket attempting a slog, his bat almost placed on top of the bails.Overton was the pick, returning his most economical figures when bowling his full allocation of four in a T20 international.Though Tom Banton dropped a catch slipping on the greasy outfield, England's fielding was otherwise exceptional.Brook took a sharp catch at mid-wicket to remove Pathum Nissanka for 36, Rashid was alert enough to run out Charith Asalanka and Dawson's direct hit was the coup de grace.At the age of 29, Donald has been given an international opportunity in this series as a replacement for Salt.He has shown only glimpses of his excellent domestic form, returning a high score of 21. On this occasion, he tried to wallop the spin of Tharindu Rathnayake over long-on and was stumped by a distance.In Buttler and Brook, the captains past and present, England have two men in supreme form. Buttler is England's best white-ball batter of all-time, while Brook is on the way to being one of their greats.Such is their quality, the second-wicket pair turned the remainder of the chase into little more than a glorified net.Sri Lanka were scruffy – they conceded 17 runs in wides. The hapless nature of the visitors' display was epitomised when Brook should have been caught off Madushanka, only for keeper Kamil Mishara and point fielder Nissanka to look at each other as the ball dropped to the ground.There was no need for Brook to attempt a single that Hasaranga fielded in his follow-through, the bowler hitting direct with a throw at the non-striker's end.Buttler won it in the following over, clubbing 18 from four Malinga deliveries, with two maximums hammered over the leg side.

schema.headline: England vs Sri Lanka: Harry Brook and Jos Buttler lead hosts to top of rankings

title: Parents could face prison for child's crimes under justice reforms, minister says
description: Parents could lose their benefits or face prison sentences for their children's crimes under reforms to the youth justice system, a minister has said.
body: Parents could lose their benefits or face prison sentences for their children's crimes under reforms to the youth justice system, a minister has said.Youth Justice Minister Jake Richards told the Times newspaper the system "should hold parents to account in a proportionate way for ensuring that they play their role in keeping communities safe".His comments come after the government set out plans in May to strengthen and expand Parenting Orders, which can currently compel parents or guardians to address their child's behaviour by attending counselling sessions or face fines.Richards said prison sentences would only apply "in the most extreme cases" and would be up to judges' discretion.He described the proposed changes in England and Wales as part of a "carrot-and-stick" approach."Parenting orders are going to make sure that parents are more involved in the process by which we try to turn around young offenders," Richards told the Times."Yes, that will have some stick. It could be custodial, or docking benefits - ultimately it will be up to a judge. But we want them to be more involved and that comes with responsibilities as well."Critics of the proposals say engaging with parents on a voluntary basis is generally more effective in building trusting relationships and providing support.Jess Mullen, chief executive of the Alliance for Youth Justice which represents more than 70 organisations that advocate for children, previously questioned how putting parents in prison would provide "stability or support for the child".Andrew Neilson, director of campaigns at the Howard League for Penal Reform, told the BBC: "Reforming parenting orders in this way risks being ineffective at best and counter-productive at worst."Criminalising parents is unlikely to help children who need support, and putting them behind bars would only put further strain on a failing prison system that is already bursting at the seams."When the government white paper was announced in May, then Justice Secretary David Lammy said that strengthening parenting orders would mean "there are real consequences for parents and carers who wilfully fail to support efforts to address their children's behaviour."He told BBC Breakfast at the time that if a parent was struggling, then the "judge can intervene to make sure that the young person is getting the support that they need and the parent is doing the best that they can". He also said he expected the power to jail parents to be used "very, very rarely".Courts are currently required to consider issuing a Parenting Order where a child under 16 has been convicted of an offence.They can also consider an order for 16 and 17-year-olds if they believe this would help prevent further offences.The term of the order must not exceed 12 months and breach of a parenting order is a criminal offence with a maximum £1,000 fine, according to the Sentencing Council. However, government statistics show the use of parenting orders has declined in recent years, from more than 1,000 orders in 2009/10 to just 33 in 2022/23.The government's youth justice reform plans come after Phase One of the Southport Inquiry report found "catastrophic" failures by the parents of the Southport killer Axel Rudakubana and various agencies meant clear chances to prevent the 2024 child murders were missed.In the interview with the Times, Richards also rejected calls from lawyers to raise the age of criminal responsibility from 10, saying it would undermine "public faith" in the justice system and it was "not a priority at all". In June, the Bar Council, the representative body for barristers in England and Wales, said the threshold should rise to 14 due to criminalisation at such an early age not being an "effective, proportionate or just response". The United Nations has previously pointed out the UK has some of the lowest ages of criminal responsibility in the world and that it should rise it to the UN recommendation of at least 14. On Thursday, ministers met with local leaders and experts in Manchester to discuss how devolution could help reform youth justice. Additional reporting by André Rhoden-Paul & Shelley Phelps, political correspondent

schema.headline: Parents could face prison for child's crimes under justice reforms, minister says

title: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I'm like my character in Sense and Sensibility
description: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I try and bury my emotion when it comes to loveImage source, Getty ImagesByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentDaisy Edgar-Jones has bee
body: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I try and bury my emotion when it comes to loveImage source, Getty ImagesByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentDaisy Edgar-Jones has been well cast in her new film.She plays Elinor, the rational elder sister in Sense and Sensibility, opposite the younger, more romantic sister Marianne.Speaking to the BBC, Edgar-Jones says that in her personal life, she really is like her character."When it comes to love, I think I am very much more Elinor in every sort of way," she says."I definitely lead a lot with my head and try and push aside, bury my emotion."But she notes that one of the joys of the film is seeing Elinor learn to enjoy a "wilder, passionate side" of herself. "And I feel like I learnt to do that too," she says.Best known for starring in hit TV series Normal People with Paul Mescal, Edgar-Jones, 28, is now taking on a lead role in the latest adaptation of Jane Austen's book.Ahead of its release, she’s been talking to me about whether we really need another Sense and Sensibility film (spoiler: yes. “The more the merrier, in my opinion.”)She also told me why young people today can still see themselves in Jane Austen's stories - and gave me her take on whether her friend and former co-star Mescal should be the next James Bond. Image source, Alex Bailey / 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLCImage caption, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles in a scene from Sense and SensibilityThe new film, directed by Georgia Oakley, follows the Dashwood sisters as they navigate their way through love, loss and societal expectations, following the death of their father.It's a classic adaptation of Austen's novel, rather than a more contemporary take.When I meet Edgar-Jones at a hotel in central London, I ask her whether there was ever a temptation to make it more "2026"."It does feel very much like it's honouring the period," she agrees, "but I think there's a freshness to the filmmaking that I think is really beautiful".She is starring alongside Esmé Creed-Miles, 26, who plays her sister Marianne.Together, the two sisters' different approaches to life are characterised as "sense" (Elinor) and "sensibility" (Marianne).Creed-Miles is also well cast, it seems. "I'm more like Marianne [than Elinor], yeah, which is annoying sometimes," she laughs.Image source, Alex Bailey / 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLCImage caption, Daisy Edgar-Jones stars as Elinor in Sense and SensibilitySense and Sensibility has been adapted for screen countless times before - including the hit 1995 film starring Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet.Edgar-Jones loves that version (“one of my favourite films of all time”) but also feels there's room to tell Austen’s classic tale again."Her stories are something that fascinate us still today,” she says.It was also easy for her and Creed-Miles to build the sisterly rapport on screen, as they previously worked together as teenagers on the 2018 film Pond Life.“We had a real laugh," Creed-Miles says of their time on that film. "We would have sleepovers every night and watch Love Island."For Edgar-Jones, the theme of sisterhood is something that stuck with her from Sense and Sensibility - despite her being an only child in real life.“I've heard a lot of people say that after watching the film, it either makes them want a sister or to ring up their sister and say like, ‘Hey, I love you,’ and I think that's really special. It's the part of the film I'm most proud of.”Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Esmé Creed-Miles and Daisy Edgar-Jones play two sisters in Sense & SensibilityJane Austen seems to be everywhere right now.Last year marked the 250th anniversary of her birth and, in recent years, we've enjoyed two BBC TV series, Miss Austen and The Other Bennet Sister, the West End's Clueless musical (based on the cult 90s teen film adaptation of Emma), and Ava Pickett's modern stage adaptation of Emma.There's also a new adaptation of Pride and Prejudice written by Dolly Alderton and starring Emma Corrin coming to Netflix.For Edgar-Jones, the themes in Austen's books are just as revelant today."She has an incredible way of articulating the female experience," she says."Her ruminations on love, on romance, on sisterly love, on family dynamics, on interpersonal social dynamics - she's such a talent."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Daisy Edgar-Jones takes a selfie with a fan at the world premiere for Sense and Sensibility in London earlier this weekAusten also wrote about the sort of dating behaviour that people complain about on TikTok (like situationships and ghosting), before terms like that had even been invented. Does that help Gen Z audiences relate to her, I ask?"Well, massively," replies Edgar-Jones."We still have the same human heart as we did 200 years ago. Our capacity to love and feel heartbreak, and that early first love feeling, is something that we all experience in various ways."And so yes, I think definitely the trials and tribulations of the two women [Elinor and Marianne] as they navigate life, love and all that becomes as you grow up, definitely is so relatable to all generations.""These women are very relatable," agrees Creed-Miles."I don't know if seeing a movie is going to fix everything, but it might make you feel a little bit less alone in some of the things you're feeling."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Paul Mescal's breakout roles were in Normal People, which came out in 2020Edgar-Jones shot to fame during the pandemic with her role in Normal People.Based on Sally Rooney's novel, the BBC Three drama charted the on-off relationship of teenagers Marianne and Connell, played by Edgar-Jones and Paul Mescal.The pair have remained close (a few years ago, Edgar-Jones told me Mescal was "one of my all-time best friends") - and both are now successful actors. Edgar-Jones has since starred in Twisters and Where The Crawdads Sing, while Mescal was in Gladiator II, Hamnet and will be in the Beatles films.Recently, Page Six claimed Mescal was on the audition list to be the next James Bond, external.So, is he really in the running? Edgar-Jones didn’t give too much away.“I don’t know, but I think there’s nothing Paul can’t do,” she says.“So I would be there. Wow, that’s cool.”Sense and Sensibility is out in UK cinemas on 25 September.

schema.headline: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I'm like my character in Sense and Sensibility

title: Ekurhuleni killings: Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
description: "What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give.""
body: "What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give.""For us, for all the other women. How many other bodies will be found before something happens?"Nokwanda is speaking to the BBC from the family home near South Africa's main city, Johannesburg, just two days after relatives identified Dineo's body.The 38-year-old mother-of-two was last seen alive on Sunday. Her battered and partly burned body was later found in the residential region of Ekurhuleni.Nokwanda weeps as she describes how the family will have to face, at some point, the grim task of telling Dineo's daughter of her death."How do you explain that your parent was brutally murdered, dumped in a field, and just left there, discarded like a piece of rubbish."There's no coming to peace with it," she adds. "It's something that you can never reconcile yourself with, that you can never get over."Dineo's death this week has come amid a series of comparable incidents in Ekurhuleni – her body one of three discovered there this week. In total, nine bodies of murdered women have been found in similar circumstances in the region since July.The problem has always been there but this spate of grim discoveries has once again sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country – which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.Themba Kekana is also living in shock at the death of a loved one.His sister, Itumeleng, was one of the first to disappear in Ekurhuleni.The 32-year-old shopkeeper's body was found in July, 17 days after she was last seen alive. Her body was badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge."We are devastated with grief," says Themba, wet eyes shining."I look at my sister's young daughter and my eyes fill with tears, I know there is no way that I can ever take this pain away from her."No family should have to deal with what we are faced with."Only one arrest has been made in connection with the murders – and that was two days after the first body was discovered on 15 July.Nobody has been detained following the murders of Itumeleng or Dineo or the other six Ekurhuleni women.Most of the victims were young, in their 20s or 30s, and almost all had suffered extreme violence before their deaths.Police have said they are not sure if they are hunting a serial killer. It is possible the cases are not linked.Either way, what has happened in this residential district east of South Africa's biggest city has traumatised the nation, shining a spotlight on a situation that many believe is a crisis.South Africa's police issue detailed crime statistics every quarter, which show that between April and June this year - 5,427 people were murdered.The official data does not distinguish between the genders of the victims, but this week the country's Human Rights Commission released figures showing that 569 women had been killed in that period (six a day on average), with another 1,052 who faced attempted murder.Many women - already feeling unsafe - have been left reeling by recent events.And it has put pressure on the government, less than a year after ministers acknowledged the scale of the issue and declared gender-based violence a national disaster.Announcing the move last November, Minister of Social Development Nokuzola Sisisi Tolashe said that treating the issue as a national disaster would help the government tackle the crisis.It followed weeks of protests, culminating in a "Women's Shut Down" march as South Africa hosted the G20 summit.This week has seen a chorus of calls for things to go further.Rights group Amnesty International said an important first step towards protecting South Africa's women was to recognise femicide as a separate crime."Every day that femicide remains unrecognised as a crime is a failure to confront the targeted killing of women," said Amnesty's country director Shenilla Mohamed in a statement. "It is time to call it what it is: Femicide."Femicide is a gender-motivated crime. It is the killing of a woman because she is a woman."Amnesty says femicide is criminalised as a specific crime in 33 countries, including Gabon and Morocco in Africa.It argues that making that change in South Africa could help focus on the scale of the issue."It would compel the state to confront their failure to protect women and girls from violence," says Mohamed. "You cannot fix what you are not tracking."Almost everyone in South Africa agrees more needs to be done.President Cyril Ramaphosa this week pledged to leave "no stone unturned" in investigating the crimes in Ekurhuleni, adding: "As a nation, we must stand up for the rights, safety and dignity of women and girls."Lebogang Ramafoko, an advocate for gender and social justice, said the levels of violence against women in the country were symptomatic of a much bigger problem – a lack of regard for humanity."The bodies of black women have been treated as disposable in this country for time immemorial, passed down from colonisation through to apartheid," she tells the BBC, referring to the legalised system of racism that was in place until 1994."What we see happening to women is testimony to legacies of violence from those systems whose traumas were never addressed."This is not to say black men are inherently violent, but in systems where violence was meted out against them for decades, historically black women were the people that that violence would be taken out on - that cycle has not been broken."In Kempton Park, a district of Ekurhuleni where five of the nine recent bodies were found, Lumka Maqhubela is part of the Girl2Woman Foundation group which has held protests to raise awareness of the crimes."We are grieved, we are scared," she says. "If the police cannot protect us any more the government should step in and do something."It's clear that we are not safe, we cannot be told by the police to be more vigilant. They should be doing more to make our communities safe – what else are we expected to do? We are not safe anywhere, not in our homes, not in the streets, it needs to stop.""I feel uncomfortable," says Thulisile Sibande, 32. "When I go to a shop, I have to look around. I'm shocked and scared. So scared, it's a trauma."Thembi Mabena, 60, tells the BBC she lived in the same neighbourhood as Dineo Motapane."She was laughing every day, with everybody," she remembers. "Now I'm worried."I know many children, girls, who tell me they are afraid to go to the shop alone. There is no safety, even for me too. I am old, but there is no safety.""In South Africa," says Lerato Mzizi, 20, simply, "women are not safe any more."

schema.headline: Ekurhuleni killings: Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa

title: From fusty to fashionable - is it cool to wear M&S clothes now?
description: Image source, Carlo Paloni/Getty ImagesImage caption, M&S show during London Fashion Week September 2026ByAnnabel RackhamCulture reporterUpdated 7 hou
body: Image source, Carlo Paloni/Getty ImagesImage caption, M&S show during London Fashion Week September 2026ByAnnabel RackhamCulture reporterUpdated 7 hours ago"I'm the first person to be like, 'It's from M&S, you need to get on to it,'" Farron Clark, a 26-year-old brand strategist tells me. According to Clark and others on social media, Marks & Spencer is becoming the hot place to shop for women under 35, while also keeping its core older audience happy too. "For a long time M&S had this fusty reputation - it was less valued by younger people," says Chioma Nnadi, head of editorial content at British Vogue, who tells the BBC there is now a "fresh energy around the brand".And accompanying that fresh energy is a new marketing strategy, which includes hosting its first-ever London Fashion Week show on Friday, featuring a collection of outfits inspired by the brand's archive.Image source, Reuters/Getty ImagesSpeaking ahead of the event at the Design Museum, the company's head of womenswear design, Lisa Illis, says they wanted to do this because of the "immediacy of seeing something and being able to own it and wear it, rather than waiting six months".For many, M&S is more synonymous with pig-shaped sweets than cutting-edge fashion, but its runway of 43 womenswear and 10 menswear looks did a lot to persuade people that the latter is where its true talent lies.Normally Fashion Week is about seeing what you'll be wearing six months from now, but this runway was full of colder weather fits, from opulent faux fur jackets and wrist cuffs, to satin jumpsuits and dresses in rich tones of navy, burgundy and brown.The catwalk featured a diverse range of models in age, size and gender, demonstrating the brand's desire to cater to a wide market. But there was certainly a concerted effort to attract the eye of younger shoppers with a fashion-forward approach to Christmas party staples like sequinned dresses, tasselled skirts and see-through lace tops.'They have created a modern version of everything we know and love'Image source, M&SImage caption, Womenswear and menswear collections at London Fashion Week are inspired by the M&S archiveThe retailer has been focusing on "newer styles and relevant trends" to attract younger customers, says Illis.But she says that this has been achieved without compromising on quality which is what keeps M&S's core audience on board."They have created a modern version of everything we know and love - cashmere staples, knitwear and the lingerie department," says Nnadi. Clark agrees that M&S has been nailing "funnel neck [styles] and barrel jeans, which are filtering down from high fashion".M&S has perhaps been fortunate to rebrand at a time when consumer habits are changing, as young shoppers consider buying capsule wardrobes - a smaller number of staple pieces that can be styled in a variety of ways. According to Clark, the idea of wear-it-once fast fashion has declined as people  "are looking for [foundational pieces] to rotate".This is something Perrie Sian, one of Britain's biggest fashion influencers, has also noticed. The 34-year-old tells the BBC: "The real height of fast fashion is behind us"."As a group we've changed our shopping habits and M&S slots into that," she says. "In my content and with lots of other creators we're showing people how to wear things in multiple ways, how to look after them."She added that she is noticing "people are willing to spend a little bit more" on wardrobe staples and items that "wash well and are made of cotton, not acrylic or polyester".Image source, Getty ImagesRevamped storesSpeaking on BBC Sounds podcast When It Hits The Fan, which she co-presents, Farzana Baduel, the president of the Chartered Institute of Public Relations, says it "hasn't always been rosy for M&S" and that past mis-steps had often led to the company being "absolutely hammered in the media"."M&S fashion, which for a while sat there like a bit of a sleepy Bagpuss on the British retail mantlepiece, has had quite a glow-up," Baduel says.During the Covid pandemic M&S struggled, but returned to growth in 2022-2023, with its fashion, home and beauty market share reaching 9.6%.This again increased in 2023-2024 to 10%, and 10.5% in 2024-2025.But the business took a big hit in 2025 due to a cyber attack, which left shoppers unable to use its website and app and affected stock in stores too.It means M&S's market share on fashion, home and beauty now sits at 10.2%, external for 2025-26.Nnadi says M&S has been investing heavily in its retail spaces in recent years, focusing on "accessible luxury" with stores that feel "welcoming, new and fresh".And that's something Clark has noticed too."Getting an iced coffee and having a walk around M&S with my friends is the perfect Saturday," she says. "My generation do so much sitting on our phones, so an in-person experience becomes a bit of an activity." Embracing young designers and collaborationsImage source, ReutersAccording to Sian, M&S has also taken "more risks" recently, which has helped it "create viral moments", including hosting a pit-lane fashion show at this year's F1 British Grand Prix and collaborating with British designers and creators."I'm seeing on Instagram or TikTok somebody say, 'Oh my goodness, this faux leather jacket is from M&S and it looks like it's £500 from the runway.' "And what am I doing? I'm hop, skip, jumping into my car and getting straight to my local M&S to hunt it down," Sian jokes. "They have embraced young designers like Marco Capaldo, the founder and creative director of 16Arlington," adds Nnadi. "And the Aries collab was genius and unexpected - it's a brand that has a lot of fashion kudos and is very British in its aesthetic but represents a younger vision of what British cool looks like," she says.Clark agrees the brand has "homed in on experts in their craft, rather than partnering with a million different people" like other fashion brands have made the mistake of doing.She notes their recent partnership with Stormzy's stylist Melissa Holbrook-Akposoe, who goes by Melissa's Wardrobe on social media, as "adding credibility" for younger shoppers.

schema.headline: From fusty to fashionable - is it cool to wear M&S clothes now?

title: Earl Spencer's Diana book opens old wounds royals would rather forget
description: At issue is Earl Spencer's account of a conversation with the then Prince Charles after the death of Diana, with the prince accused of telling Earl Sp
body: At issue is Earl Spencer's account of a conversation with the then Prince Charles after the death of Diana, with the prince accused of telling Earl Spencer: "We'll forget her soon enough."He is accused of sounding "giddily elated" and like a "lottery winner" after the news of her death.Buckingham Palace hit back with a response, which although dressed in courtier-like politeness, was essentially saying the conversation had never happened like that.The King was said to be "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways that others do not recognise".Anyone who has lost someone knows how feelings can run high, people can hear different things about the same conversations - and families can fall out, or come together, in the wake of a death.Psychotherapist Nick Hatter says he doesn't have a view on which version of events is correct, but he says that during traumatic events memories can be "distorted". A phone call doesn't have any of the visual clues or body language to give a fuller picture, he adds.Hatter says there can be very different and unpredictable responses to grief, including a condition known as "bereavement mania" where someone can seem inappropriately hyper or even euphoric after the loss of a loved one.The first opinion poll on who to believe has been published by YouGov - and it suggests a very split view, with 31% believing Earl Spencer's allegations, 36% suspecting it's not true and 33% saying they don't know.Low thinks the book is unlikely to change many opinions, as "people have settled into their camps about how they regard Charles, how they look back on the Diana years".There could also be a feeling that it's "tawdry" to rake up these claims so many years later, he says.That's echoed by historian and author Sir Anthony Seldon who says Earl Spencer showed great courage at the time of Diana's funeral, but says his memoir is a "sad and unnecessary publication".Royal commentator Richard Palmer says the book threatens to take the royals back to the difficult days of 1997."This book and the run-up to next year's 30th anniversary of Diana's death threaten to undermine the Royal Household's three decades of work to rehabilitate Charles and Camilla's image," he says.Veteran broadcaster David Dimbleby, who led the BBC's coverage of Diana's funeral, said it seemed "odd" Earl Spencer would release the book now. "Why 30 years later for God's sake you should do it... you have to ask him,"  he said on Radio 4's Today programme, adding he wished the appetite for the "cycle of gossip" would decline and instead that focus would shift to what kind of monarchy the country needed. Earl Spencer, in a statement ahead of the book's launch, said he had been "inundated" with requests for interviews about his sister, with the upcoming 30th anniversary prompting him to write down his own memories "rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths that have become accepted over time". He is fiercely defending the accuracy of his claims, in interviews over the weekend, including with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.In it Earl Spencer doubles down on his allegations about King Charles, saying: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said."I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

schema.headline: Earl Spencer's Diana book opens old wounds royals would rather forget

title: An American found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and hopes others do too
description: I found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and I want others to do the sameFigure caption, "It was very serendipitous" - Mary and Jason on findin
body: I found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and I want others to do the sameFigure caption, "It was very serendipitous" - Mary and Jason on finding love in IrelandBySheila FlynnSenior US ReporterMary Timby was fed up with dating apps when she booked a trip to Ireland on a whim last summer - from the comfort of her Colorado couch.The spur-of-the-moment trip was unlike her: Timby, 39, is a self-described "total planner". But she'd always wanted to visit Ireland, and she found herself exhausted by the local dating scene while navigating a career transition. And then she remembered a few throwaway lines from a comedy series about a matchmaking festival in Ireland.So she looked it up - and not only was the Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival real, it was also taking place during the entire month of September, when she was scheduled to visit.Now, a little more than a year later, Timby is reaping the benefits of that uncharacteristic last-minute decision: She's become a viral star. She's found love with an Irishman she met at a pub called The Matchmaker. And she's even started a new business venture - bringing others to Lisdoonvarna who hope to follow in her footsteps.Image source, Mary TimbyImage caption, Timby and Jason Mangan, 38, from County Clare, Ireland, are pursuing a transatlantic romance"It's really about enjoying County Clare, enjoying the festival, and, if you meet someone, you do - and that's what happened with us," says Timby, smiling at her partner, Jason Mangan, sitting beside her.They're speaking from the windswept coastal cottage they rented together for the summer in his native County Clare - about 20 miles (32 km) southwest of Lisdoonvarna, the site of their first fortuitous meeting.'Mary, your video is going viral'From the outset, Timby's inaugural Ireland trip seemed to take on a life of its own.She filmed a short video on the plane before her flight took off, telling her approximately 300 TikTok followers that she was heading on an off-the-cuff trip to an Irish matchmaking festival - and didn't "know what's going to happen".Timby then "turned my phone on airplane mode, then spent about eight hours on the flight (and) woke up at Shannon Airport," she says.When she turned on her phone, "it was blowing up".A group of friends had texted her. "They said, 'Mary, your video is going viral,'" she says. "I didn't even have notifications on for social media."She rented a manual transmission car - horrified to find the gear stick on the left side of the driver's seat - and set off through County Clare to her accommodation at an Irish family's home. Then she headed to Lisdoonvarna, where she saw firsthand that the festival is a whole-town, month-long celebration of conversation and dancing, rather than a line of singles waiting to be set up by a sage local matchmaker.Image source, Mary TimbyImage caption, Colorado woman Mary Timby, 39, visited Ireland's Aran Islands with her new beauThat's changed since the festival's origins 170 years ago, when bachelor farmers and moneyed visitors would flock to the spa town of Lisdoonvarna to bathe in its mineral-rich waters and socialise. Generations of matchmakers would ply their trade to set up successful marriages, and word spread. Now, while the town's year-round residents number fewer than 1,000, up to 80,000 visitors descend upon Lisdoonvarna from around the world each September.Third-generation matchmaker Willie Daly still holds court at his nearby home and at festival events, and Timby even visited him during her trip - when he put her on the phone to random men whose accents she struggled to understand.But the real magic of contemporary Lisdoonvarna lies in the town's overflowing streets and pubs - as Timby soon found out.Her first night in town was "a little slow," she admits - and Timby was tired and jet-lagged. She retired to her room and spent the next day sightseeing, but the Irish woman running her accommodation convinced her to try Lisdoonvarna again that night."My AirBnB host said, 'You should go back tonight, because I heard that the younger folks come out at night,'" laughs Timby.So she did - and found herself dancing and drinking pints at The Matchmaker Bar in the centre of town. That's when a "handsome Irishman" approached her.'Conversation just flowed'"I went over and introduced myself, and... conversation just flowed," says Mangan, 38, from Ennis, County Clare, about 22 miles southeast of Lisdoonvarna. He'd been to the festival before and was well-acquainted with its cultural significance, remembering his grandparents making the journey decades earlier for the dancing."Unfortunately, I didn't have much time on my hands, because I was turning back to Ennis," says Mangan, designated driver that night for a group of friends. "So I got her name, and I said, 'Oh, sure, I might see you around.'"It was a very short interaction, to be honest with you."Image source, Mary TimbyImage caption, The couple first met at Lisdoonvarna's Matchmaker Bar during the annual festivalHe didn't leave it at that, though; Mangan found Timby on Instagram and followed up with a message inviting her out."It was short and sweet, and it was really genuine, too," says Timby - and she took him up on the offer.What followed was a series of whirlwind dates - lunches, dinners, sightseeing and shopping trips. Timby extended her time in Ireland and documented much of it for her newfound following - but she didn't reveal anything about her new beau. They wanted to save the burgeoning romance for themselves.When Timby eventually had to fly home, there were "tears at the airport" - but they decided to keep the relationship going."It was very tough to say goodbye," Timby says. "It was very tough to start a long-distance relationship, but it ended up being a really good opportunity for us to sort of slow things down a bit."They kept talking daily, Mangan impatiently waiting for Timby to wake up seven hours behind him in Colorado. She flew back to Ireland again, then he made his first trip to America for Thanksgiving 2025. Timby returned to Ireland at Christmas and met his family, and after that, they decided to make her boyfriend's big social media reveal."We thought, this is something we already know we want to invest in... we were ready to share," Timby says. "So New Year's Eve, we shared a photo of him, and people were just over-the-moon excited."The pair watched their following grow, drawing interest from Irish cafes and tourist destinations to the local Gaelic sports club in Colorado. Their story also caught the attention of Lisdoonvarna locals, who approached Timby - a communications consultant - about being an ambassador for the festival."So I said: Sign me up," Timby laughs. "I love the festival. It brought me Jay."Image source, Mary TimbyImage caption, Mangan has made repeated trips to Colorado since their 2025 meeting in IrelandTimby's been inundated with messages from lovelorn followers hoping to replicate her matchmaking success."I heard from many of my followers... groups of people wanting to go to the festival but not having anyone to go with" or "not knowing what to do," Timby says. "I really listened to that, and I also wanted to be mindful of the fact that I love Ireland."I'm so excited to showcase County Clare and all the amazing things that the west coast of Ireland has, but I'm also not a tour operator."So she partnered with a company called Met Through Friends, which organises and encourages real-life meetups for people looking for love. They released an interest form for a trip, expecting "80 to 100 responses." They received 560.The first group of eight will make the trip later this month, with Timby's Irish boyfriend consulting on the itinerary."You can go on all these apps, swipe left, swipe right, but it's not actually going out and making a connection with someone and experiencing a small little town in Ireland, experiencing the culture," says Mangan."It's a once-in-a-lifetime experience... you never know."Timby, smiling at her boyfriend of one year, agrees."I echo everything Jay just said," she says. "Put your phone down and put yourselves out there, and good things will come."

schema.headline: An American found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and hopes others do too
